title: might
subtitle: I might go
summary: Use might + verb to say that something is possible: I might go = it is possible that I will go.

lesson.heading: It is possible
lesson.text: A woman in a travel agent's asks a man: 'Where are you going for your holidays?' He thinks about a big city with tall buildings and says: 'I'm not sure. I might go to New York.' Outside, a woman looks up at dark clouds and says: 'It might rain.' **might** + verb says that something is possible.

examples.note: = it is possible that he will go to New York
= it is possible that it will rain

lesson.heading: The form
lesson.note: might is the same for every subject: he **might go**, not ~~he mights go~~ or ~~he might goes~~.

lesson.heading: I might = it is possible that I will
lesson.text: We use **I might** when we are not sure. It means: perhaps I will, it is possible that I will.

examples.text: **I might go** to the cinema this evening, but I'm not sure.
examples.note: = it is possible that I will go

examples.text: *A:* When is Rebecca going to phone you? *B:* I don't know. She **might phone** this afternoon.
Take an umbrella with you. It **might rain**.
Buy a lottery ticket. You **might be** lucky.

lesson.heading: I might not
lesson.text: **I might not** = it is possible that I will not.

examples.text: I **might not go** to work tomorrow.
examples.note: = it is possible that I will not go

examples.text: Sue **might not come** to the party.
examples.note: = it is possible that she will not come

lesson.heading: may
lesson.text: You can use **may** in the same way. **I may** = **I might**. And **May I ... ?** = Is it OK to ... ? / Can I ... ?

examples.text: I **may go** to the cinema this evening.
Sue **may not come** to the party.

examples.note: = is it OK to ask / can I ask?

lesson.text: After might there is no *to*: I might go, not ~~I might to go~~.

exercises.prompt: It's possible that I'll see you tomorrow. ___ you tomorrow.
exercises.explanation: might + verb says that something is possible.

exercises.prompt: It's possible that Sarah will forget to phone. Sarah ___ to phone.
exercises.explanation: might is the same for every subject: Sarah might forget.

exercises.prompt: It's possible that it will snow today. It ___ today.
exercises.explanation: It might snow = it is possible that it will snow.

exercises.prompt: Somebody is asking about your plans. You have some ideas, but you are not sure. Match each question with your answer.

pairs.left: Where are you going for your holidays?
pairs.right: I'm not sure. I might go to Italy.

pairs.left: What are you doing at the weekend?
pairs.right: I don't know. I might go away.

pairs.left: What are you going to have for dinner?
pairs.right: I don't know. I might have fish.

pairs.left: How are you going to get home tonight?
pairs.right: I'm not sure. I might take a taxi.

pairs.left: What are you going to do with the money you won?
pairs.right: I haven't decided yet. I might buy a new car.

exercises.prompt: It's possible that Mark will not be here next week. Mark ___ here next week.
exercises.explanation: might not = it is possible that ... will not.

exercises.prompt: It's possible that you won't have time to go out. Say it with might not.
exercises.answer: I might not have time to go out.
exercises.explanation: might not + verb, with no to after might.

exercises.prompt: You ask Bill: 'Are you going to get up early tomorrow?' Bill says: 'Perhaps.' What do you write about Bill?
exercises.explanation: 'Perhaps' means Bill is not sure, so we use might.

exercises.prompt: You ask Bill: 'Will you be at home tomorrow morning?' Bill says: 'Maybe.' So he ___ at home tomorrow morning.
exercises.explanation: 'Maybe' = it is possible, so: He might be at home.

exercises.prompt: You ask Bill: 'Are you working tomorrow?' Bill says: 'No, I'm not.' What do you write about Bill?
exercises.explanation: Bill is sure, so we don't use might: He isn't working tomorrow.

exercises.statement: You ask Bill 'Are you going out in the afternoon?' and he answers 'Yes, I am.' So: He might go out in the afternoon.
exercises.explanation: He's going out in the afternoon. Bill is sure, so might is wrong here.

exercises.prompt: Is the speaker sure, or is it only possible?

items.text: Rebecca is going to phone later.
Sue might not come to the party.
He's going out in the afternoon.

exercises.prompt: You are in a class and you want to ask something. What do you say?
options: May I to ask a question?
exercises.explanation: May I ... ? = Is it OK to ... ? After may we use the verb with no -ing and no to.
